what_its_for: Dalbavancin is an antibiotic used to treat certain serious skin and skin-structure infections caused by bacteria, including infections caused by MRSA (a type of staph bacteria that is hard to kill). It helps fight the infection by stopping the bacteria from growing.
how_to_take: Dalbavancin is NOT a pill or liquid you take at home. It is given through an IV (intravenous) line directly into your vein by a nurse or doctor in a clinic, hospital, or infusion center. Each treatment takes about 30 minutes. You will likely only need one or two doses total, which makes it very convenient compared to many other antibiotics.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the exact dose based on your weight and medical condition. The most common dosing schedule is either: (1) a single dose of 1,500 mg given one time, OR (2) two doses — 1,000 mg on Day 1, followed by 500 mg one week later. Your doctor will choose the schedule that is best for you. Do not try to change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by a healthcare provider in a clinic or hospital setting, a missed dose is uncommon. However, if you miss your scheduled infusion appointment, call your doctor or infusion center right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Do not skip or delay your dose without talking to your healthcare team first, as this could allow your infection to get worse.
storage: You do not need to store this medication at home — it is prepared and stored by the healthcare facility or pharmacy that gives it to you. If for any reason you are given prepared medication to bring to an infusion site, keep it refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C) and do not freeze it. Use it within the timeframe your pharmacist tells you.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL medications, vitamins, and supplements you take before receiving dalbavancin. Avoid starting any new medications without telling your doctor first. Do not skip follow-up appointments, as your doctor needs to check that your infection is healing properly. If you have a known allergy to vancomycin or other glycopeptide antibiotics, make sure to tell your healthcare team before receiving this medicine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following: a skin rash, hives, or severe itching; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; difficulty breathing or swallowing; redness, flushing, or hives during or after the infusion (this can be a sign of a reaction sometimes called 'Red Man Syndrome'); severe diarrhea or stomach cramps, especially if you see blood or mucus in your stool (this could be a serious bowel infection); signs your skin infection is getting worse such as increasing redness, warmth, swelling, or pain; fever, chills, or feeling very unwell; yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or unusual tiredness (signs of liver problems).
when_it_works: Because dalbavancin stays in your body for a long time, it begins working against the infection right away after your first dose. Many patients start to feel better within a few days. However, it is important to keep all follow-up appointments so your doctor can confirm the infection is fully treated, even if you feel better quickly.
special_populations: Kidney problems: If you have moderate to severe kidney disease and are not on dialysis, your doctor may give you a lower dose. Make sure your doctor knows about any kidney problems before you receive this medicine. Liver problems: Use with caution if you have severe liver disease; your doctor will decide if this medicine is right for you. Pregnancy: It is not fully known if dalbavancin is safe during pregnancy. Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: It is not known if dalbavancin passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Dalbavancin can be used in children and adolescents under 18 for certain infections; the dose will be calculated based on the child's weight. Elderly patients (65 and older): No special dose adjustment is needed based on age alone, but your doctor will consider your overall health and kidney function.
